Pultusk Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Pułtusk, Poland

Demolished. Jewish settlement in Pułtusk developed after 1808; by 1921, 5,919 Jews made up nearly 44% of the town's population. In September 1939, Germans deported all of Pułtusk's Jews to Warsaw and Soviet-occupied territory, and most who remained in Poland were later murdered. The cemetery was established in the 1820s on land donated by Zelman Lubranitzer. Officially, the site had been considered closed since 1940; a 1956 plowing incident and subsequent 1957 and 1960 closure applications by local authorities described it as abandoned, with traces of graves nearly invisible, and slated for housing development. A formal liquidation decree followed in 1963, and a factory (later 'Polam-Pułtusk') was built directly on the site. Surviving tombstones were stored at the Regional Museum and State Archives in Pułtusk until, in 2012, the local Academy of Humanities unveiled a monument built from tombstone fragments on the small undeveloped remnant of the original grounds.
